scope.start: 8a: Rami bar Chama's inference that one who lifts a find for another makes him acquire (after the previous daf's discussion of dividing by value)
scope.end: 8b: the Mishnah's two riders explained as two kinds of leading (the baraita of the camel and donkey follows on 8b–9a)

sections.title: *Magbiah metziah le'chavero*: Rami bar Chama's Principle or Rava's Migo
sections.gist: Rami bar Chama infers from the Mishnah that one can lift a find for another. Rava holds that the Mishnah proves only *migo*, and applies it to a *cheresh* and a *pikeach*. The Gemara then searches the Mishnah's clauses for Rami bar Chama's source.

children.title: Rami bar Chama: Two Lifting Together Proves One Lifts for Another
children.gist: If *magbiah metziah le'chavero* (lifting for another) did not work, two who lift a garment together would each hold a half 'as though lying on the ground', and a third party could take it; so each must be lifting for the other.

bullets.text: Rami bar Chama infers from the Mishnah (2a): *ha'magbiah metziah la'chaveiro kanah chaveiro*. One who lifts a find on behalf of another makes the other its owner.

Why this is new despite *zakhin le'adam she'lo be'fanav*: lifting a find for someone also shuts out everyone else who might take it. One could think a person may do that for himself but not, at others' expense, for someone else.
The proof: were it not so, when two lift a garment together, each one's half would be 'as though lying on the ground'. Neither would acquire, and a third party who took it would keep it.
Since the Mishnah has them divide it, each must be lifting for the other as well.
Each finder really wants the find for himself. But the *kinyan* works only if each also acts for the other, so we assume that he does.

illustration.caption: Rami bar Chama's inference (8a): two finders each hold half a garment. If one could not lift a find for another, each half would be 'as though lying on the ground' and a third party could take it. Since the Mishnah has them divide, each lifts for the other.

children.title: Rava: Not *magbiah metziah le'chavero*, but Migo; the Agent and the Partners
children.gist: Rava says the Mishnah proves only that one who acquires for himself can acquire for another too (*migo*). He shows it from partners who steal: only one lifts the item, yet both are liable.

bullets.text: Rava: one who lifts a find solely for another does not make him acquire it. The Mishnah's finders acquire because each acquires part for himself, and so (*migo*) he acquires the other part for his fellow.
Proof: one who tells his agent 'go out and steal for me' is exempt when the agent steals, since there is no agency for a sin (*ein shaliach li'dvar aveirah*).

Yet partners who steal together are both liable even if only one of them lifted the item. The reason: since he acquires for himself, he acquires for his partner too. The Gemara concludes that the principle is correct.

Rava's claim is narrower than Rami bar Chama's. *Migo* lets one attach another's acquisition to one's own. It proves nothing about a person with no stake acquiring a find purely for another, which is where the harm to third parties is sharpest.

illustration.caption: Rava's proof for *migo* (8a). When an agent steals for his sender, the sender is exempt. When partners steal and only one lifts the item, both are liable: since he acquires for himself, he acquires for his partner.

children.title: Cheresh and Pikeach Lift a Find: Both, Only the Cheresh, or Neither?
children.gist: Rava applies *migo* to a *cheresh* and a *pikeach* who lift a find together. The Gemara revises his ruling twice and concludes that neither acquires, then explains why two chereshim are different.

bullets.text: By Torah law a *cheresh* cannot make an acquisition. The Sages let him keep what he finds, for the sake of peace, but only for himself and not on behalf of others.
Rava: since the *cheresh* acquires his part, the *pikeach* also acquires his.

Challenge: the *cheresh* acquires because the *pikeach*, acquiring for himself, lifts the rest for him. But the *pikeach* needs the *cheresh* to acquire for him, and a *cheresh* cannot acquire for another.
Restated: the *cheresh* acquires and the *pikeach* does not. The *migo* here is different: two chereshim who lift a find together acquire it, so this *cheresh* does too.
Challenge: even Rami bar Chama's rule applies only when one lifts intending the other to acquire. The *pikeach* lifted for himself. If he does not acquire for himself, would he acquire for others?
Conclusion: since the *pikeach* does not acquire, the *cheresh* does not either.

Why two chereshim are different: the Sages gave them the find so that they would not come to quarrel. Here the *cheresh* reasons, 'if even the *pikeach* does not acquire, can I?', and will not quarrel.
No unfairness calls for a remedy here. The *cheresh* is no worse off than the *pikeach* beside him, so the Sages' ordinance need not be stretched to cover him.

The *pikeach* acquires nothing, so no one lifts the rest for the *cheresh*

children.title: Where in the Mishnah? Four Clauses Deflected, the Last One Holds
children.gist: Rav Acha son of Rav Adda asks Rav Ashi which clause Rami bar Chama infers from. The opening case, the repeated 'all mine', the 'half mine' claim and the riders are each deflected. The clause about agreement or witnesses proves it, though Rava reads that clause as *migo*.

chart.caption: The Mishnah's clauses tested as Rami bar Chama's source
columns: Why it might be the source
rows: Two holding a garment (opening case)
The basic case of two finders
Each claims he lifted all of it; nothing about lifting together
'All of it is mine' / 'all of it is mine'
Seems to repeat the opening case
The opening case is a find; this one is a purchase
'All of it is mine' / 'half of it is mine'
Seems to add nothing
May be a purchase; teaches that the half-claimant still swears, since he may be using a ruse
Two riding an animal
Seems to add nothing
Teaches that one sitting on an animal acquires it
They agree, or have witnesses: divide without an oath
For a purchase this would be obvious, so it must be a find lifted together
Accepted as the source; Rava reads it as *migo*

children.title: Opening Case and 'All Mine' Twice: A Find and a Purchase
children.gist: In the opening case each claims he lifted the whole garment. The repeated 'all mine' clause was already explained on 2a as a purchase, so it is not superfluous.

bullets.text: Rav Acha son of Rav Adda to Rav Ashi: where does Rami bar Chama's inference come from? Not the opening case. There each says 'all of it is mine, and I lifted all of it', which says nothing about lifting together.

Suggestion: the clause 'this one says all of it is mine and that one says all of it is mine' seems superfluous after 'I found it'. So it must teach that even if they lifted it together they divide, and a third party cannot take it.
Answer: the Gemara already established (2a) that the first clause speaks of a find and the later one of buying and selling.

children.title: 'All Mine' vs. 'Half Mine': A Ruse to Escape the Oath
children.gist: The 'half mine' clause may also be a purchase. It would then teach that the one claiming half still swears, since he may be avoiding the oath by a ruse (*arumei ka me'arim*).

bullets.text: Suggestion: 'all of it is mine' vs. 'half of it is mine' adds nothing to the earlier cases, so learn from it that *magbiah metziah le'chavero* works.
Challenge: why assume this clause is about a find? It may be about buying and selling.
Then its point is this: one might think the half-claimant is like one who returns a lost item (*meshiv aveidah*). He could have claimed all of it, so he should be exempt from an oath.
The Mishnah teaches that he is not exempt. He may be using a ruse (*arumei ka me'arim*): 'if I claim all of it I must swear; I'll claim half, look like one returning a lost item, and be exempt.'
By claiming all he would receive half; by claiming half he receives only a quarter. Giving up that quarter is a plausible price for escaping an oath.

children.title: Two Riding an Animal: Perhaps It Teaches That Riding Acquires
children.gist: The riders' clause seems redundant, but it may teach that one who sits on an animal acquires it even without making it move.

bullets.text: Suggestion: two sitting on an animal, each claiming it, swear and divide its value. The case adds nothing, so it must be the source for lifting on another's behalf.
Answer: it may teach that one who sits on an animal acquires it, even though he has not made it move.
The standard acquisition of an animal is making it move (*meshikhah*), so acquisition by merely sitting would be a real novelty of its own.

children.title: Agreement or Witnesses: The Proof Found, and Rava's Migo Reading
children.gist: Dividing without an oath when they agree or have witnesses would be obvious for a purchase, so the clause must speak of a find they knowingly lifted together. Rava reads the same clause as *migo*.

bullets.text: The last clause: when they admit each other's claims, or have witnesses, they divide without an oath.
For a purchase, this would go without saying. So it speaks of a find, and they divide because they knowingly lifted it together, intending both to acquire. This proves Rami bar Chama's rule.
Rava answers that the clause rests on *migo*: since each acquires for himself, he acquires part for the other as well.
Rava accepts that two who lift together each acquire half. He denies only that one person with no stake of his own can acquire a find for another at the expense of others.

returns_to.note: Rava's *migo* reading, first stated at 8a.6, answers the proof found in this clause

sections.title: Riding or Leading: Which Acquires an Animal, and Which Prevails?
sections.gist: Shmuel's half-remembered rulings on *rakhuv* and *manhig* turn into a question of which prevails. Then come Rav Yehuda's proof from *kilayim*, Abaye's challenge about the reins, the law of *moseirah*, and the Mishnah's two riders.

chart.caption: Acts of acquisition for an animal, as the Gemara has them so far
rows: Leading (*manhig*) by pulling
Yes
A standard acquisition; no one says leading fails
Sitting in riding position (*rakhuv*) alone
Not by Rav Yehuda's proof; still being tested
Shmuel's version of Kilayim 8:3: the one sitting in the wagon is exempt, so sitting is no act
Holding the reins, taken from another
Yes
The other hands them over (Rav Huna; Idi)
Holding the reins of a found animal or a convert's estate
No
Rav and Shmuel; Idi's *baraita*: no one hands them over
Riding while driving with the legs
Yes, a second kind of leading
The Mishnah's two riders; no stronger than leading by the reins

children.title: Shmuel's Forgotten Rulings: Rider vs. Leader, Who Takes Precedence?
children.gist: Rav Yehuda heard from Shmuel that one of *rakhuv* and *manhig* acquires and one does not. Since leading surely acquires, the doubt must be about a rider and a leader of the same animal.

bullets.text: The Mishnah: two sitting on an animal, or one sitting and one leading, each claiming it, both swear and divide.

Rav Yosef: Rav Yehuda told me he heard two rulings from Shmuel, on one sitting in riding position (*rakhuv*) and on one leading (*manhig*). One acquires and one does not, and he did not know which is which.

Each one alone? No one says leading alone fails to acquire, since pulling or leading an animal is a classic acquisition. If either failed it would be the rider, and there would be nothing to be unsure about.
So the question is a rider together with a leader. Does the rider prevail, since the animal is in his grasp, or the leader, since it walks because of him?
Terms: one who actively rides, driving the animal, shades into leading. *Rakhuv* is one merely seated on the animal without driving it.

illustration.caption: The case behind Shmuel's forgotten rulings (8b): one person sits on the animal while another leads it. Does the rider prevail because the animal is in his grasp, or the leader because it walks because of him?

children.title: Rav Yehuda's Proof from Kilayim: The Wagon-Sitter Is Exempt
children.gist: In Shmuel's version of Kilayim 8:3 the Sages exempt one sitting in a wagon drawn by animals of two kinds. So for Shmuel sitting is no act: a rider does not acquire on his own, still less against a leader.

bullets.text: Rav Yehuda: though I don't remember what Shmuel said, let us reason it out from Mishnah Kilayim 8:3. When animals of two kinds pull a wagon, the one leading them incurs forty lashes, and so does the one sitting in the wagon. R. Meir exempts the one sitting.
Shmuel taught the Mishnah reversed: 'and the Sages exempt the one sitting in the wagon.' Since the halakha follows the Sages against R. Meir, he evidently holds that sitting is no act.
Conclusion: one who sits on an animal alone does not acquire it, and all the more so when another is leading it.

Tosafot's bridge between *kilayim* and acquisition: the sitter makes the animals move a little, a kind of *meshikhah*. If that small movement does not count as driving for *kilayim*, it is no meaningful *meshikhah* for acquisition either.
The proof yields more than the question asked. It is not that the rider loses to the leader; riding by itself is no *kinyan* at all.

illustration.caption: Mishnah Kilayim 8:3 as Rav Yehuda uses it (8b): animals of two kinds pull a wagon. The leader incurs lashes. The one sitting in the wagon is liable in the Mishnah as usually taught, but in Shmuel's version the Sages exempt him, so sitting is no act.

children.title: Abaye Challenges Rav Yosef: Whose Proof, and Wagon vs. Saddle
children.gist: Abaye doubts that the proof was Rav Yehuda's. In two versions the objection about the reins is raised and answered: holding the reins of an ownerless animal does not acquire it.

bullets.text: Abaye to Rav Yosef: many times you told us this reasoning as your own, never in Rav Yehuda's name. Rav Yosef had lost his memory through illness.
Rav Yosef: indeed, I remember that Rav Yehuda said it, and that I objected. One sitting in a wagon does not hold the reins; one sitting on the animal does.
Rav Yehuda answered him: Rav and Shmuel both say that holding the reins of an ownerless animal does not acquire it. So sitting on the animal is no different from sitting in the wagon.
Another version: Abaye himself raised the objection about the reins, and Rav Yosef answered with Idi's *baraita*: holding the reins of an ownerless animal does not acquire it.
Zero plus zero is zero. If sitting adds nothing and the reins add nothing, a rider holding the reins still has no *kinyan*.

children.title: Moseirah: Reins Acquire from a Seller, Not a Find or a Convert's Estate
children.gist: Rav Huna: holding the reins acquires an animal from another person but not an ownerless one. As Idi explained, reins work by being handed over.

bullets.text: R. Chelbo in the name of Rav Huna: the reins (*moseirah*) acquire when taken from another person. With a found animal, or the estate of a convert who died without heirs, they do not.

Rava: Idi explained to me that *moseirah* is 'like a person who hands over (*moser*) an item to another.' From another person, the owner hands him the reins. With a find or a convert's estate, who is handing them to him?
The force of *moseirah* lies in the act of transfer, not in the grip. With no one transferring, taking hold of the reins is merely holding them.

illustration.caption: Rav Huna's ruling on the reins, as Idi explained it (8b). A buyer who takes the reins from the seller acquires, because they are handed to him. One who takes hold of the reins of a found animal or a convert's estate does not.

children.title: The Mishnah's Riders: Leading with the Legs, Two Kinds of Manhig
children.gist: The Mishnah's riders seem to show, following the Sages, that riding acquires. The Gemara answers that the rider drives the animal with his legs: a second kind of leading, which does not outrank leading by the reins.

bullets.text: Challenge from the Mishnah: whose view is it? For R. Meir even one sitting in a wagon acquires the animal pulling it, so there would be no need to teach riding. It must be the Sages, and then riding acquires.
Answer: the rider here is leading with his legs, squeezing or kicking the animal so that it moves.
Then isn't that simply leading? The *tanna* teaches two kinds of leading: pulling by the reins, and driving the animal from its back.
One might say the rider prevails, since he both leads and holds the reins. The Mishnah teaches that his claim is no stronger than that of the one leading by the reins.
This settles Shmuel's question of precedence in the Mishnah's own case. The two forms of *manhig* are equal, so the two claimants divide.

returns_to.note: The riders' clause, earlier suggested as teaching that sitting acquires, is now read as leading with the legs
Answers, for the Mishnah's case, whether the rider takes precedence over the leader

children.continues: Continues on 8b–9a: a baraita on two people pulling a camel or driving a donkey, and R. Yehuda's view, tested for whether riding acquires.

key_terms.sense: lifting a find on another's behalf
key_terms.definition: The question whether one who lifts an ownerless found object on behalf of another person thereby makes that person its owner, even though this shuts others out from taking it.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rami bar Chama infers from the Mishnah that the other acquires; Rava holds the Mishnah proves only that one acquiring for himself can acquire for another.

key_terms.sense: acquiring for another by acquiring for oneself
key_terms.definition: The principle that since a person acquires an item for himself, he can at the same time acquire part of it on behalf of another.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rava's alternative explanation of the Mishnah's two finders, proven from partners who steal and tested on a cheresh and a pikeach lifting together.

key_terms.definition: A deaf-mute, whom halakha treats as lacking the understanding needed for full legal acts; the Sages gave him limited powers, such as keeping what he finds, for the sake of peace.
key_terms.on_this_daf: A cheresh and a pikeach who lift a find together: after two revisions the Gemara concludes neither acquires, unlike two chereshim.

key_terms.definition: Acquiring a movable object or an animal by pulling it or making it move into one's control.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The backdrop to whether merely sitting on an animal, without making it move, can acquire it.

key_terms.sense: sitting on an animal to acquire it
key_terms.definition: Sitting astride an animal in riding position as a proposed act of acquiring it, as distinct from leading or pulling it.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Shmuel's forgotten ruling, Rav Yehuda's proof that riding alone does not acquire, and the Mishnah's riders read as leading with the legs.

key_terms.sense: leading an animal to acquire it
key_terms.definition: Driving or leading an animal so that it moves because of the person, a standard way of acquiring an animal.
key_terms.on_this_daf: No one doubts that leading acquires; the question is whether it prevails over a rider, and the Mishnah turns out to teach two equal kinds of leading.

key_terms.definition: Taking hold of an animal's reins as an act of acquiring it; its force rests on the reins being handed over by the owner.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Holding the reins acquires from a seller but not a found animal or a convert's estate, which answers Abaye's wagon-versus-saddle objection.

key_terms.sense: working animals of two kinds together
key_terms.definition: The Torah prohibition of plowing or pulling with two different species of animal together, as with an ox and a donkey.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Shmuel's version of Kilayim 8:3, exempting one sitting in the wagon, is used to show that sitting on an animal is no act of acquisition.

judgment_calls: The cheresh-and-pikeach discussion could stand as its own top-level section; it is kept under the Rami bar Chama / Rava discussion because it is Rava's own extension of *migo* and serves the same question.

The search for Rami bar Chama's source in the Mishnah (8a.14–23) could be a separate top-level section. It is nested under the same discussion because it tests his inference and ends with Rava's *migo* answer, linked back with returns_to.
The two versions of the Abaye–Rav Yosef exchange are kept in one section with a chart, not split into two children, since both reach the same answer about the reins.

The Mishnah's challenge from the riders (8b.11–12) could be its own section outside the riding discussion; kept as its last step because it answers Shmuel's question of precedence, with returns_to links to s8 and s11.
The riders' clause at 8a.20–21 is left in the source search where it falls, not moved to the riding discussion.
coverage_notes: 8a.1–8a.3 (division means dividing the value) belongs to the previous daf's scope and is covered in its essay tail; not outlined here.
8b.13 (the baraita of pulling a camel and driving a donkey) is outside this scope and not in the essay; noted in `continues`.
The essay says each partner who steals carries part of the item; the text says both are liable even if only one of them lifted it. Followed the text.
The essay says Rava concludes that the two situations must be kept distinct; the text concludes 'learn from it that this principle (migo) is correct'. Followed the text.

The essay explains the restated ruling (cheresh acquires, pikeach does not) as the pikeach lifting for the cheresh; the text gives the migo that two chereshim who lift together acquire. Followed the text.

The essay credits the answer to Abaye's reins objection to Idi. In the text's first version, Rav Yehuda answers in the name of Rav and Shmuel; Idi's baraita appears only in the second version. Followed the text.
The essay does not mention Abaye's challenge about attributing the proof to Rav Yehuda (Rav Yosef's memory loss), which is in the text; outlined from the text.
The essay skips the step at 8a.18 where the Gemara suggests the 'half mine' clause may speak of buying and selling; outlined from the text.
The quarter share of the half-claimant (s7) comes from the shiur's account of the Mishnah and is marked as shiur.
